transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-28
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Miguel Torres (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (Redwood Eng Ops), Priya Patel (Acme Head of ML), Tom Reed (Acme Infra), Samantha Li (Acme CTO)

Summary (auto): quick review of benchmarks vs baseline provider, some noisy transcription, action items captured at end.

[00:00] Ava Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, happy Wednesday. quick check of who we have, priya, tom, sam?
[00:06] Priya Patel: yes i'm here, sorry running a bit late, caught the tail of the last email.
[00:09] Tom Reed: here, good to go.
[00:11] Samantha Li: on the call as well.
[00:13] Ava Chen: great, i'll hand to miguel to walk through the benchmark slides and the numbers vs your baseline provider x. miguel?
[00:18] Miguel Torres: cool thanks ava. alright so i pulled together the runs from monday and tuesday, we ran the same request mix you sent over — mostly chat completion style, avg token length ~120, prompts with two-step tool calls, and the concurrency profile matched your staging traces at 120 rps peak.
[00:32] Miguel Torres: first top-line: on our dedicated config with 2x A100-equivalent instances and q4 quant profiles, p50 is about 42ms, p95 is ~85ms, and sustained throughput was around 1.2k reqs per second before we saw queueing. baseline provider x reported p95 ~110ms and throughput ~900 rps under your trace.
[00:52] Tom Reed: sorry real quick, those p95 numbers are tokens or request-level?
[00:55] Miguel Torres: good question — request-level end-to-end generation latency measured from request arrival to final chunk delivered. token latency inside can vary but the p95 i quoted is the whole response.
[01:05] Priya Patel: that's promising, but what's the tail behavior at high concurrency? your p99?
[01:09] Miguel Torres: p99 for the dedicated run was around 220ms, that was when we hit the autoscaling boundary and started to get a small backlog. note that with prefix caching — sorry K-V cache — we saw better tails for repeated prompts.
[01:22] Jordan Park: i want to call out that the cache is a K-V cache not KV cash, the transcripts earlier had a typo but it's a key-value cache for prefix tokens, it's what reduces repeat work.
[01:31] Samantha Li: can you explain quickly the difference in config between your run and ProviderX? like are they using same quant and batch sizes?
[01:37] Miguel Torres: short answer: not exactly. ProviderX by default had a larger batch target and no prefix caching enabled for their managed endpoint. their quant was a 16-bit float path for those runs — we matched inference accuracy by using q4 range (4-bit) on our runtime which gives us better throughput at similar quality profile.
[01:54] Tom Reed: wait q4 versus fp16 — i thought lower-bit quant would harm quality, did you run any evals on the prompt sets?
[02:00] Miguel Torres: yes we ran the rubric you shared — accuracy degradation under q4 was within the tolerance you specified (less than 1.5% regression on your eval set). we can share the per-prompt diffs in the spreadsheet.
[02:11] Priya Patel: please do. also the baseline provider had a note about their network egress being colocated, could your infra have any advantage because it's colocated with the dataset?
[02:21] Ava Chen: to be clear the dedicated test was in the same cloud region as your staging traces — we matched region to minimize network differences. we also tried a hosted run where region mismatch added ~10-20ms to p50.
[02:33] Miguel Torres: yea hosted adds more network variability. dedicated keeps latency predictable.
[02:36] Priya Patel: understood. what about batching settings? you said you changed them — what's the effective batch size?
[02:42] Miguel Torres: for those peak runs we targeted dynamic batching with a max batch size of 64 and a batching window of 12ms. ProviderX was running max 128 with 25ms window, which increases throughput but raises latency tail.
[02:56] Tom Reed: ah that makes sense. are these batching settings something we can tune in the cockpit?
[03:00] Miguel Torres: absolutely yes, redwood console exposes batching config per route, and the suggestions engine in Redwood Optimize recommended the 64/12ms tradeoff for your workload.
[03:10] Samantha Li: any notes on cold starts / model load times? we saw sporadic spikes on baseline during scale events.
[03:17] Miguel Torres: for dedicated we preload model shards so cold starts were <2s for scale events because of warm pool; ProviderX had on-demand spin-ups that occasionally hit 6-8s. we also have auto-warm policies for expected traffic bursts.
[03:30] Ava Chen: quick interjection — priya you mentioned success metrics earlier; are we still targeting 100ms p95 as your SLO?
[03:37] Priya Patel: yes that's the target. ideally we'd like under 80ms but 100ms is acceptable. more important is consistency.
[03:44] Miguel Torres: on dedicated we're comfortably under 100ms p95 in these runs. on hosted you see ~110-130 depending on region.
[03:52] Tom Reed: curious about cost delta, like what's the per-token or per-request delta compared to ProviderX at this config?
[03:59] Ava Chen: we'll send the detailed cost worksheet, but top-level, with caching and batching optimizations we estimate a 15-25% lower unit cost than the baseline under your workload pattern. invoice-level pricing for dedicated also has commit tiers.
[04:13] Priya Patel: ok that's helpful. i want to dig into security — are audit logs and KMS integrated for private deployments? provider x sells that but we need evidence.
[04:22] Miguel Torres: yes private and dedicated both support customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations, and comprehensive audit logs. we have SOC2 type II attestation and we can share the security pack.
[04:32] Samantha Li: can we get the security docs today? like the compliance pack?
[04:35] Ava Chen: yes i'll share our security deck and SOC2 report after the call. we'll put links in the follow-up email.
[04:42] Priya Patel: thanks. back to benchmarks — did you run the baseline provider's endpoint side-by-side or are you using their published numbers?
[04:49] Miguel Torres: we ran side-by-side hitting ProviderX's managed endpoint with the same request stream; to be fair, ProviderX's default settings weren't tuned for your workload so we also ran them with a tuned config. tuned ProviderX did improve throughput but still the p95 tail remained higher, mainly due to the batching/window choices and lack of prefix cache.
[05:07] Tom Reed: one more perf detail — what about GPU utilization? are you seeing headroom?
[05:11] Miguel Torres: good point — during the runs our GPU utilization was around 65-78% on average; there is headroom for short bursts, but at sustained 1.2k rps we start approaching 85-90% which is where queueing starts to show. that said, autoscaling within the dedicated pool added capacity before the queue grew too large.
[05:28] Jordan Park: note that utilization reporting in our instrumentation has ~1-2% variance vs cloud metrics.
[05:33] Priya Patel: did you test different quantization libs? sometimes the vendor-specific kernels make a difference.
[05:39] Miguel Torres: we tested two quant libs — our optimized kernel path and a community runtime — the optimized path on our runtime gave 10-12% better throughput. community path was ~on-par with ProviderX.
[05:51] Samantha Li: any red flags? like failure modes we should be worried about?
[05:55] Miguel Torres: observed one edge case when prompt length spikes to 600 tokens, latency jumps naturally; we recommend route-level max tokens and graceful degradation. also occasional tokenization mismatch for a tiny subset of inputs — we logged those and will include fixes.
[06:10] Priya Patel: ok good. for the soak test — what's the plan? how long and what config?
[06:15] Ava Chen: plan is 24 hours on dedicated using the committed instance profile we discussed (2x A100-equivalent) with q4 quant, batching 64/12ms, prefix cache enabled, and the real request trace you provided. we'll capture p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU utilization, error rates and memory stats.
[06:31] Tom Reed: do you need creds to our staging to run it directly, or will you replay traces from your side?
[06:36] Miguel Torres: we can run both — replay from our side is quicker but running against your staging is better to capture network and infra differences. ideally priya provides staging access for a read-only test account.
[06:47] Priya Patel: i'll get that to you by friday, devops will make a test user.
[06:51] Samantha Li: timeline for soak results?
[06:53] Ava Chen: we aim to start the soak the week of 6/2 and have preliminary results by 6/5. follow-up call on 6/6 to review.
[06:59] Priya Patel: sounds good. any other asks from your side?
[07:02] Miguel Torres: please share any additional heavy prompts — especially multi-turn threads — because caching helps more there. and if you have a few hundred real examples that trigger edge tokenization we want to include them.
[07:15] Priya Patel: will do.
[07:17] Tom Reed: regarding pricing, can you share a sample committed pricing sheet for dedicated? we might need to run procurement.
[07:24] Ava Chen: yes i'll attach a tentative committed pricing and the consumption model; that said we can discuss discounts based on commit.
[07:31] Samantha Li: one quick question on data retention — provider x claims ephemeral retention for hosted, but we need logs for debugging. what's your default retention and can we customize?
[07:41] Miguel Torres: default logs retained 30 days but enterprise plans can configure longer retention and export to your S3 or SIEM. audit logs are retained per contract.
[07:49] Priya Patel: ok fine.
[07:51] Ava Chen: alright let's recap action items and next steps quickly.
[07:55] Miguel Torres: action items: i'll run the lower-batch perf test variant and share results by 6/4; ava will send the benchmark spreadsheet, security pack, and committed pricing by 5/30; priya will provide staging access and additional traces by 5/29. schedule follow up for 6/6 to review soak.
[08:15] Priya Patel: sounds right. thanks everyone.
[08:18] Tom Reed: thanks.
[08:19] Samantha Li: thanks all. end.
